subject: Medicine
summary: Chronic Kidney Disease (CKD) is persistent kidney damage or eGFR <60 mL/min/1.73 m² for ≥3 months. Progressive nephron loss leads to complications like anaemia, bone disease and cardiovascular risk.

sections.p: CKD is defined by kidney damage (proteinuria, imaging, histology) or an estimated GFR below 60 mL/min/1.73 m² persisting for at least three months.
b: eGFR calculated with CKD‑EPI or MDRD equations; use race‑neutral formula when possible.

t.b: What is the current kidney function? Low eGFR confirms CKD; trends show progression.
What is kidney size/structure? Small, shrunken kidneys support chronic disease; enlarged kidneys suggest PKD or diabetic nephropathy.

sections.p: CKD is staged by eGFR and albuminuria, guiding prognosis and management.
b: Stage 1: eGFR ≥90 with evidence of damage.
Stage 2: eGFR 60‑89 with damage.
Stage 3a: eGFR 45‑59.
Stage 3b: eGFR 30‑44.
Stage 4: eGFR 15‑29.
Stage 5: eGFR <15 (kidney failure).

sections.p: Identify the underlying aetiology to target therapy; consider common and tropical causes.
b: Diabetic nephropathy – most frequent worldwide.
Hypertensive nephrosclerosis – second most common.
Chronic glomerulonephritis (e.g., post‑infectious, IgA).
Polycystic kidney disease – hereditary, often presents with enlarged kidneys.
Obstructive uropathy – stones, strictures, congenital anomalies.
Infections prevalent in low‑resource settings: HIV‑associated nephropathy, TB‑related renal disease, schistosomiasis, malaria‑induced nephropathy.
Herbal nephrotoxins and chronic NSAID use.

sections.p: Early CKD is often silent; later stages produce systemic signs.
b: Asymptomatic proteinuria or incidental low eGFR.
Fatigue, loss of appetite, pruritus from uremia.
Edema, especially periorbital or pedal, from sodium retention.
Anemia‑related pallor, dyspnea on exertion.
Bone pain, fractures from secondary hyperparathyroidism.

sections.p: Select tests that answer specific clinical questions; adapt when resources are limited.
b: Baseline labs to assess function, anemia, mineral bone disorder.
Imaging to evaluate size and obstruction.

t.b: Is there anemia? Low hemoglobin suggests reduced EPO; treat with ESA if needed.
Is secondary hyperparathyroidism present? Elevated PTH with low calcium indicates need for vitamin D analogues.
What type of kidney injury? RBC casts suggest glomerulonephritis; granular casts suggest tubulointerstitial disease.
Are kidneys small (chronic) or enlarged (PKD, diabetic)? Guides further work‑up.

sections.p: Recognise life‑threatening sequelae that need urgent action.
b: Rapid eGFR decline >5 mL/min/1.73 m² in 2 weeks.
Severe hyperkalemia (>6.5 mmol/L) with ECG changes.
Pulmonary edema or hypertensive emergency.
Uremic pericarditis, encephalopathy, or refractory nausea/vomiting.

sections.p: Treat the cause, slow progression, and manage complications.
b: Control blood pressure <130/80 mmHg; ACE inhibitors or ARBs preferred for proteinuria reduction.
Tight glycemic control (HbA1c ≈ 7%) in diabetic CKD.
SGLT2 inhibitors (e.g., dapagliflozin) when eGFR ≥30 mL/min/1.73 m² to reduce progression and heart‑failure risk.
Low‑protein (0.8 g/kg) diet with adequate calories; avoid excess sodium.
Treat anemia with iron supplementation and erythropoiesis‑stimulating agents if Hb < 10 g/dL.
Manage mineral bone disorder: phosphate binders, active vitamin D, calcimimetics as needed.
Avoid nephrotoxins (NSAIDs, contrast) and adjust drug doses to eGFR.

sections.p: Regular monitoring detects progression and complications early.
b: Every 3‑6 months: eGFR, ACR, blood pressure, electrolytes.
Annually: CBC, calcium/phosphate/PTH, lipid profile.
Vaccinate against hepatitis B, influenza, pneumococcus.
Educate patients on lifestyle: low‑salt diet, smoking cessation, regular exercise.

sections.p: Distinguish CKD from acute kidney injury and other chronic renal disorders.
b: Acute kidney injury – rapid rise in creatinine, often reversible.
End‑stage renal disease – CKD stage 5 requiring dialysis or transplant.
Nephrotic syndrome – heavy proteinuria with edema but may have normal eGFR early.

sections.p: Be aware of false‑normal or misleading findings.
b: eGFR may overestimate function in low muscle mass; consider cystatin C if available.
Serum creatinine can be normal in early CKD if hyperfiltration masks damage.
Urine dipstick may miss low‑level albuminuria; use quantitative ACR.

whenToSeekHelp: Sudden worsening of kidney function, severe hyperkalemia, pulmonary edema, hypertensive emergency, uremic pericarditis, or any rapid change in mental status.

faq.q: Why is proteinuria important in CKD?
faq.a: It signals ongoing kidney damage and predicts faster progression; reducing proteinuria improves outcomes.
Early stages can stabilize or improve with strict control of blood pressure, glucose, and avoidance of toxins, but established nephron loss is permanent.
Typically when eGFR <15 mL/min/1.73 m² with symptoms (uremia, fluid overload, refractory hyperkalemia) or when complications cannot be managed medically.

exam: Describe the diagnostic criteria and staging system for CKD.
List the three most common causes of CKD worldwide and two tropical infections that can lead to CKD.
Explain why ACE inhibitors are first‑line for proteinuric CKD and how SGLT2 inhibitors add benefit.

sections.h: Bedside: history and how to examine
sections.p: A focused history and systematic exam reveal the chronicity, aetiology and complications of CKD and guide which investigations are needed.
b: Onset and duration of renal symptoms; ask about gradual fatigue, swelling, change in urine volume or colour
Past medical history: diabetes, hypertension, HIV, TB, known kidney disease, recurrent urinary infections
Medication review: ACE‑I/ARB, diuretics, NSAIDs, herbal remedies, nephrotoxic antibiotics
Family history of polycystic kidney disease or hereditary nephropathies
Social history: occupation (exposure to heavy metals), water source, use of traditional medicines
Pregnancy history and obstetric complications
Dietary intake of protein, salt and potassium
Symptoms of complications: bone pain, pruritus, dyspnoea, nocturia, haematuria

t.b: Look for pallor, cachexia, peripheral oedema, periorbital puffiness; presence suggests anaemia or volume overload
Detect hypertension (≥140/90 mmHg) which is both cause and consequence of CKD; uncontrolled BP worsens progression
Identify volume overload or uremic cardiomyopathy; S3 suggests fluid overload
Enlarged kidneys (palpable flank mass) point to polycystic disease or hydronephrosis; a scar may suggest prior surgery

t.a: Peripheral pulses and peripheral oedema grading
t.b: Assess severity of fluid retention; pitting oedema >1 cm indicates significant sodium retention
Crackles indicate pulmonary congestion from fluid overload
Asterixis suggests uremic encephalopathy; hyperreflexia may reflect electrolyte disturbance
Detect proteinuria, haematuria, glucosuria, nitrites; a positive protein strip (>1+) supports renal damage but cannot quantify albuminuria

sections.h: Investigations and how to read them
sections.p: Select tests that answer a specific clinical question; when a test is unavailable use a surrogate or clinical judgment.
b: Serum creatinine and eGFR (CKD‑EPI, race‑neutral) – answers kidney filtration; eGFR < 60 mL/min/1.73 m² defines CKD

t.b: Answers current filtration; Jaffe may be falsely high with hyperbilirubinaemia or ketoacidosis – use enzymatic if available
Detect hyperkalaemia, metabolic acidosis; K > 5.5 mmol/L contraindicates potassium‑rich fluids
Identify anaemia; Hb < 12 g/dL in women or < 13 g/dL in men suggests CKD‑related anaemia
Answers structural cause; echogenic kidneys with loss of corticomedullary differentiation suggest chronic disease; hydronephrosis points to obstruction
Kidney length < 9 cm supports advanced CKD; enlarged kidneys (>13 cm) suggest polycystic disease
Detect dysmorphic RBCs (glomerulonephritis) or casts (granular, waxy) indicating chronic damage
Low (<3.5 g/dL) indicates malnutrition or protein loss, worsens prognosis
Identify infectious contributors; positive HIV may imply HIV‑associated nephropathy
Look for cardiomegaly or pulmonary congestion secondary to fluid overload

sections.p: CKD is diagnosed when structural damage or reduced filtration persists for ≥3 months; staging combines eGFR and albuminuria to predict outcomes.
b: eGFR ≥ 60 mL/min/1.73 m² with persistent proteinuria or imaging abnormality → CKD stage 1
eGFR 60‑89 mL/min/1.73 m² with damage → CKD stage 2
eGFR 45‑59 mL/min/1.73 m² → CKD stage 3a
eGFR 30‑44 mL/min/1.73 m² → CKD stage 3b
eGFR 15‑29 mL/min/1.73 m² → CKD stage 4
eGFR < 15 mL/min/1.73 m² → CKD stage 5 (kidney failure)

sections.p: Several disorders mimic CKD clinically or biochemically; careful history, targeted tests and bedside clues separate them.

t.b: Rapid rise in creatinine over days; urine output < 0.5 mL/kg/h; no chronic structural changes on imaging – differentiate by time course
Elevated creatinine with volume overload; presence of S3, pulmonary crackles, and normal kidney size on ultrasound – consider cardiac origin

t.a: Nephrotic syndrome secondary to primary glomerulonephritis
t.b: Heavy proteinuria (>3.5 g/day) with oedema but eGFR often preserved early; kidney biopsy needed to differentiate from CKD progression

t.a: Chronic liver disease with hepatorenal syndrome
t.b: Low urine sodium (<10 mmol/L), high creatinine, absence of structural kidney disease on US, and advanced cirrhosis signs – distinguishes from intrinsic CKD

sections.p: A structured ladder guides CKD care from stabilising the patient to definitive renal replacement, with clear triggers for escalation and referral.
b: 1. Confirm diagnosis, stage, and reversible causes; counsel on lifestyle, low‑salt diet, avoid nephrotoxins.
2. Optimise blood pressure (<130/80 mmHg) and glycaemic control; start ACE‑inhibitor or ARB for proteinuria >300 mg/day.
3. Add SGLT2 inhibitor if eGFR ≥30 mL/min/1.73 m² and diabetes or albuminuria, for renal protection.
4. Treat anaemia with oral iron; consider erythropoietin when Hb <10 g/dL and iron replete.
5. Manage mineral‑bone disorder: give active vitamin D analogue and phosphate binders when serum phosphate >5.5 mg/dL or PTH elevated.
6. Monitor eGFR, urine albumin‑creatinine ratio, electrolytes, haemoglobin, calcium‑phosphate‑PTH every 3‑6 months; adjust meds accordingly.
7. Escalate to nephrology when eGFR <30 mL/min/1.73 m², refractory hypertension, uncontrolled hyperkalaemia, or rapid decline >5 mL/min/yr.
8. Prepare for renal replacement (dialysis or transplant) when eGFR <15 mL/min/1.73 m² or symptomatic uremia.

sections.h: Drug effects and what to do
sections.p: Key adverse effects, drug‑drug interactions and practical steps to mitigate them in CKD.
b: ACE‑inhibitor/ARB: may cause hyperkalaemia and rise in serum creatinine ≤30 %; hold if K⁺ >5.5 mmol/L or creatinine ↑>30 % from baseline.
SGLT2 inhibitor: risk of genital mycotic infection; ensure good hygiene, treat early; stop if eGFR falls <30 mL/min/1.73 m².
Loop diuretics: can cause ototoxicity with high doses; monitor hearing and electrolytes, avoid concurrent aminoglycosides.
Phosphate binders (calcium‑based): risk of hypercalcaemia; check calcium quarterly, avoid in adynamic bone disease.
Active vitamin D analogue: may cause hypercalcaemia and hyperphosphataemia; monitor Ca and P, reduce dose if Ca >10.2 mg/dL.
Erythropoietin stimulating agents: raise blood pressure and thrombosis risk; treat hypertension first, use lowest effective dose.

sections.p: Recognise life‑threatening or rapidly progressive complications that demand urgent referral or change in management.
b: Severe hyperkalaemia (K⁺ >6.5 mmol/L) or ECG changes – give calcium gluconate, insulin‑glucose, consider dialysis.
Acute rise in creatinine >30 % with volume overload – assess for acute tubular necrosis, obstruction, or drug toxicity; refer urgently.
Refractory hypertension (>150/95 mmHg despite three agents) – evaluate secondary causes, intensify ACE‑I/ARB, consider renal denervation referral.
Symptomatic anaemia (Hb <8 g/dL) with cardiac strain – start erythropoietin and transfusion if needed, refer to nephrology.
Severe secondary hyperparathyroidism (PTH >800 pg/mL) with bone pain – add calcimimetic, consider parathyroidectomy referral.
Uremic pericarditis (sharp chest pain, friction rub) – initiate dialysis urgently.

sections.p: Conditions that alter presentation, laboratory interpretation, or therapeutic choices in CKD.
b: HIV: may cause HIV‑associated nephropathy; ART drugs (e.g., tenofovir) are nephrotoxic – monitor eGFR and switch if decline.
TB: anti‑TB drugs (rifampicin, isoniazid) can raise transaminases and interact with warfarin; adjust doses for eGFR <30 mL/min/1.73 m².
Malnutrition: low albumin falsely lowers eGFR estimates; supplement protein 0.8‑1.0 g/kg/day while avoiding excess phosphorus.
Pregnancy: physiological GFR rise masks CKD; use cystatin C‑based eGFR if available; avoid ACE‑I/ARB, switch to labetalol for hypertension.
Diabetes: tight glycaemic targets (HbA1c 7‑8 %) reduce progression; avoid metformin if eGFR <30 mL/min/1.73 m².
Herbal nephrotoxins (e.g., aristolochic acid) – obtain thorough medication history, counsel cessation.
Alcohol: binge drinking worsens hypertension and liver disease; advise ≤14 units/week.
Advanced liver disease: low albumin skews creatinine‑based eGFR; consider measured clearance or cystatin C.

sections.p: Tailored considerations for children, pregnant women, the elderly, HIV‑positive patients and low‑resource environments.
b: Children: use height‑based Schwartz formula for eGFR; stage by eGFR and proteinuria; prioritize growth‑promoting nutrition and avoid nephrotoxic antibiotics.

Pregnancy: monitor serum creatinine each trimester; treat hypertension with labetalol or nifedipine; give calcium‑based phosphate binders only if needed, avoid vitamin D analogues that cross placenta.
Elderly: start ACE‑I/ARB at low dose, watch for orthostatic hypotension; prioritize fall‑prevention, consider frailty when deciding dialysis timing.
HIV‑positive: use renal‑sparing ART (e.g., dolutegravir); screen for proteinuria quarterly; vaccinate against hepatitis B and pneumococcus.
Low‑resource settings: use dipstick proteinuria and bedside eGFR calculators; employ cheap phosphate binders (calcium carbonate); arrange peritoneal dialysis if haemodialysis unavailable.

sections.p: Sample questions covering bedside assessment, investigations, management decisions and special‑population issues.
b: 1. Which bedside sign distinguishes ascites from pleural effusion? Explain the technique and its limitation.
2. A patient with eGFR 28 mL/min/1.73 m² has serum potassium 6.2 mmol/L and peaked T waves. What immediate steps do you take?
3. How does the Jaffe method for creatinine measurement mislead in a CKD patient with high bilirubin?
4. When serum phosphate rises above 5.5 mg/dL in stage 4 CKD, which medication class should be added and why?
5. A pregnant woman with CKD stage 2 presents with hypertension. Which antihypertensive agents are safe and which must be avoided?
6. Explain how HIV infection modifies the interpretation of protein‑creatinine ratio in CKD.
7. List the criteria for diagnosing CKD in children and how they differ from adults.
8. A 70‑year‑old on ACE‑I develops a rise in creatinine from 1.2 to 1.6 mg/dL. What is the appropriate management?
9. Which oral hypoglycaemic is contraindicated when eGFR falls below 30 mL/min/1.73 m² and why?
10. Describe the nutritional modifications for a child with CKD stage 3 regarding protein, sodium, and phosphorus.

facts: eGFR <60 mL/min/1.73 m² for ≥3 months defines CKD regardless of cause.
ACE‑I or ARB are first‑line for proteinuric CKD; they reduce intraglomerular pressure and slow progression.
SGLT2 inhibitors add 30‑40 % eGFR preservation on top of ACE‑I/ARB in diabetes or albuminuric CKD.
Serum potassium >5.5 mmol/L is a contraindication to potassium‑rich fluids in CKD.
Anemia in CKD is defined as Hb <13 g/dL (men) or <12 g/dL (women) after correcting iron deficiency.
Secondary hyperparathyroidism appears when 1,25‑(OH)₂ vitamin D <20 pg/mL and phosphate >4.5 mg/dL.
Kidney‑derived 1‑α‑hydroxylase converts 25‑OH vitamin D to active 1,25‑(OH)₂ vitamin D.
Urea cycle: excess amino acids → ammonia → urea via carbamoyl phosphate synthetase I in liver mitochondria.
Low‑resource CKD work‑up: dipstick protein, point‑of‑care creatinine, urine ACR, blood pressure, hemoglobin.

vivas.q: Define chronic kidney disease according to KDIGO.
vivas.a: Kidney damage (proteinuria, imaging, histology) or eGFR <60 mL/min/1.73 m² for ≥3 months.

vivas.q: What are the five CKD stages based on eGFR?
vivas.a: Stage 1 ≥90, Stage 2 60‑89, Stage 3a 45‑59, Stage 3b 30‑44, Stage 4 15‑29, Stage 5 <15 mL/min/1.73 m².

vivas.q: Which fluid is safest for a CKD patient needing maintenance IV fluids but who must avoid excess potassium?
vivas.a: 0.45 % saline (half‑normal saline) – provides volume without adding potassium.

vivas.q: Why is the Jaffe method for creatinine measurement problematic in advanced CKD?
vivas.a: It overestimates creatinine due to non‑specific chromogens, especially when serum creatinine is high, leading to inaccurate eGFR.

vivas.q: Which hepatic pathway converts excess amino acids into ammonia and then urea?
vivas.a: The urea cycle in the liver mitochondria and cytosol.

vivas.q: What active hormone must the kidney hydroxylate for calcium‑phosphate balance?
Initial medical therapy for secondary hyperparathyroidism in stage 4 CKD with high PTH?
vivas.a: Start active vitamin D analog (calcitriol or alfacalcidol) and control phosphate with binders.

vivas.q: What direct complication of progressive CKD explains fatigue and pallor?
Which medication is contraindicated in patients with nephrolithiasis or moderate‑severe CKD?
vivas.a: NSAIDs – they reduce renal prostaglandins, worsening GFR and promoting stone formation.

vivas.q: List the five CKD stages based on GFR for paediatric patients.
vivas.a: Stage 1 ≥90, Stage 2 60‑89, Stage 3 30‑59, Stage 4 15‑29, Stage 5 <15 mL/min/1.73 m², same as adults.

vivas.q: What are the main aetiologies of paediatric CKD by age group?
vivas.a: Infants: congenital anomalies (CAKUT); 1‑5 y: hereditary diseases (PKD, Alport); >5 y: glomerulonephritis, obstructive uropathy, infections.

vivas.q: Key nutritional recommendations for children with CKD.
vivas.a: Adequate energy (30‑35 kcal/kg), protein 0.8‑1.0 g/kg (adjusted for stage), restrict sodium, phosphorus, and potassium as needed; supplement vitamin D and iron.

vivas.q: What bedside test helps differentiate pruritus from uremic itch?
vivas.a: Inspection for excoriations; uremic itch often worsens at night and improves after dialysis, not linked to skin rash.

vivas.q: How would you assess volume status in a CKD patient at the bedside?
vivas.a: Inspect for edema, measure jugular venous pressure, auscultate lung bases for crackles, palpate hepato‑jugular reflux; positive signs indicate fluid overload.

vivas.q: When is renal biopsy indicated in CKD in low‑resource settings?
vivas.a: When the aetiology remains unclear after basic labs, especially if rapid decline, proteinuria >1 g/day, or suspicion of treatable glomerulonephritis.

vivas.q: Why must ACE‑I/ARB be held before a contrast study?
vivas.a: They can precipitate acute kidney injury by blunting autoregulation when renal perfusion falls.

vivas.q: What is the first‑line phosphate binder in CKD‑MBD when calcium load must be limited?
vivas.a: Sevelamer – a non‑calcium polymer binder effective without raising serum calcium.

vivas.q: How does HIV infection modify CKD assessment?
vivas.a: HIV can cause proteinuric nephropathy; antiretroviral drugs may affect creatinine assays and eGFR; monitor CD4 and viral load alongside renal parameters.

mcqs.q: A 58‑year‑old man with diabetic CKD stage 3b presents with serum potassium 6.2 mmol/L. Which medication should be stopped immediately?
mcqs.e: ACE‑I can raise potassium; stopping it reduces hyperkalaemia risk.

mcqs.q: Which of the following is the most reliable method to estimate GFR in a malnourished African patient when creatinine assays are limited?
mcqs.e: Cystatin C is less affected by muscle mass and diet, giving a better estimate in malnutrition.

mcqs.q: A CKD patient on dialysis develops bone pain, low calcium and high phosphate. Which hormone is deficient?
mcqs.e: Kidneys fail to hydroxylate vitamin D, causing low 1,25‑(OH)₂ vitamin D.

mcqs.q: Which of the following is contraindicated in a patient with known bilateral renal artery stenosis?
mcqs.e: ACE‑I can precipitate acute renal failure in bilateral renal artery stenosis.

mcqs.q: In a low‑resource clinic, a patient with CKD has a urine dipstick showing 2+ protein and a serum creatinine of 2.5 mg/dL. What is the next best step?
o: Begin ACE‑I and arrange follow‑up ACR
mcqs.e: ACE‑I addresses proteinuria; ACR quantifies albuminuria for staging.

mcqs.q: Which drug class is most likely to cause analgesic nephropathy in chronic NSAID users?
mcqs.e: Chronic non‑selective NSAIDs reduce prostaglandin‑mediated renal blood flow, leading to chronic interstitial nephritis.

cases.v: A 12‑year‑old boy from a rural area has recurrent urinary tract infections, bilateral hydronephrosis on ultrasound, and serum creatinine 1.8 mg/dL. He reports occasional flank pain.

qs.q: What is the most likely underlying cause of his CKD?
qs.a: Obstructive uropathy due to posterior urethral valves or congenital ureteric obstruction.

qs.q: What bedside examination finding would support chronic obstruction?
qs.a: Palpable, non‑tender kidneys with a firm, enlarged flank mass; bladder distension may be present.

qs.q: What is the next investigative step in a low‑resource setting?
qs.a: Perform a voiding cystourethrogram or, if unavailable, refer for surgical assessment and possible catheter drainage.

mistakes: Confusing eGFR cut‑offs for CKD staging with those for acute kidney injury; CKD requires chronicity ≥3 months.
Using serum creatinine alone to stage CKD in malnourished or muscular patients; ignore muscle mass effect.
Prescribing ACE‑I/ARB without checking baseline potassium or serum creatinine, leading to hyperkalaemia or AKI.
Failing to adjust phosphate binders when calcium‑based binders are already raising serum calcium.
Assuming all proteinuria is glomerular; missing orthostatic proteinuria or overflow from myeloma.
Neglecting to screen for HIV, TB, or schistosomiasis in endemic areas, which can alter management.
Over‑relying on dipstick protein without confirming albuminuria; dipstick may miss low‑grade albuminuria.
Starting high‑dose steroids without a biopsy confirmation in presumed glomerulonephritis, risking infection.
